first_impression.reaction: My assistant put this in front of me because my fiance's family is Latvian on his mother's side. The first screen is calm and a little bit sharp: "Baltic wedding traditions are usually served up as one list, as if Tallinn, Riga and Vilnius shared a single rulebook. They don't." That's confident without being eager. Still, it's a culture guide. I'd skim the rest for any sign these people can run something our size.

journey.quote: Baltic wedding traditions are usually served up as one list, as if Tallinn, Riga and Vilnius shared a single rulebook. They don't.
journey.reaction: Good. It doesn't lump everyone together, which my future mother-in-law would notice immediately.

journey.section: Baltic wedding traditions: three countries, three sets of customs
journey.quote: Where a custom is passed on by word of mouth rather than documented, we say it is "often told", and we leave its meaning to your family.
journey.reaction: That's the cultural respect I look for. They aren't telling the family what its own customs mean.

journey.quote: Treat it as a fixed midnight moment in the run sheet, and ask early whether a folklore group can perform.
journey.reaction: Practical, and it sounds like someone who has actually written a run sheet. This is the one custom his family would insist on.

journey.section: 8. Gates and obstacles on the way (Lithuania)
journey.quote: Build slack into your transfer times, and give the best man something to hand over at each gate.
journey.reaction: Charming, but it's written for one car and a best man with a bottle. With 300 guests and private transfers, road stops become a security question. Nothing here tells me they've thought about that.

journey.quote: Treat Kihnu as a living community to learn from, with local permission, rather than a backdrop.
journey.reaction: I like this. It's the opposite of the influencer approach, and it suggests they won't turn a family's culture into content.

journey.quote: Two more entries belong to the wider culture, not to the wedding itself.
journey.reaction: This is where my assistant stopped summarising. The UNESCO section is thorough, but it's more than I need. It reads like a reference page, not a planner.

journey.quote: For a Latvian wedding, look at Riga and other places well away from that border area.
journey.reaction: Sensible and plainly said. But safety for us means our own security team working with the venue's, and that isn't mentioned anywhere.

journey.quote: If the Baltics are one option among several, our [European destination weddings](/blog/europe) and [destination wedding packages](/destination-wedding-packages) show how a wedding abroad comes together.
journey.reaction: 'Packages' again. That word tells me I'd be slotted into a tier. My assistant wouldn't click it.

journey.section: Bringing Baltic customs to a wedding at home
journey.quote: One person is your single point of contact, and the fee and inclusions are agreed in writing before any work begins.
journey.reaction: Grown-up, no discount talk. One contact suits how we work. It still says nothing about discretion.

unanswered_questions: Has Wedded Wonderland delivered a wedding of 200 to 400 guests, in the Baltics or anywhere else?
Can they secure exclusive use of a manor or estate near Riga for several days, and work alongside our own security team?
How do they protect privacy: NDAs, guest phone policies, keeping vendors and folklore performers off social media?
Can they arrange private transfers and VIP arrivals for guests flying in from Dubai, London and Sydney?
Is there a private or referral channel to someone senior, rather than a general advisor link?

turn_offs_found.quote: If the Baltics are one option among several, our [European destination weddings](/blog/europe) and [destination wedding packages](/destination-wedding-packages) show how a wedding abroad comes together.
turn_offs_found.why: Package language makes it sound like a standard tier, which is exactly what we don't want.

would_share_with: My fiance's mother, for the Latvian mičošana section
My assistant, to file with the planner shortlist notes

cta_reaction.quote: If you are planning a wedding in the Baltics, or a Baltic-Australian celebration at home, you can [speak with a Wedded Advisor](/wonderland-concierge?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=content&utm_campaign=baltic-wedding-traditions&utm_content=bridge).
cta_reaction.why: The tone is calm and there's no hard sell, and the closing line about 'a calm place to start' suits me. But I don't fill in web forms. If my assistant could get a private introduction, I'd take a call. On this page alone, I've no evidence of scale or discretion.

top_3_changes: Swap the 'destination wedding packages' link for a page that doesn't say 'packages', such as a bespoke or concierge planning page.
Add one understated line near the bridge saying the team handles exclusive use, private transfers and security liaison for larger family weddings, if that's true.
Mention discretion or privacy in the CTA, and offer a private conversation rather than only a general advisor link.
